title: A bison in the grasslands of Theodore Roosevelt National Park, North Dakota
caption: The giant that came back
subtitle: National Bison Day
description:
When the going gets tough, the bison gets grazing. National Bison Day celebrates the North American mammal that can weigh up to 2,000 pounds yet sprint at 35 mph. Observed on the first Saturday of November, the day honors the bovine that became the United States' national mammal in 2016.
Despite often being called a buffalo, the American bison is not one of the true buffaloes, which are native to Africa and Asia. Its scientific name, Bison bison, leaves little room for confusion. Its muscular shoulder hump helps it swing its head side to side, clearing snow to reach grass underneath. Both males and females grow horns and beards. Their tails offer clues about their mood: a swishing tail generally signals calm, while a raised tail may indicate agitation.
Yellowstone National Park is the only place in the United States where bison have lived continuously since prehistoric times. Once nearly driven to extinction, bison have made an impressive conservation comeback. Today, their survival is a conservation success worth celebrating.

title: Lanterns for Diwali, Mumbai, Maharashtra, India
caption: A celebration that shines
subtitle: Diwali (Festival of Lights)
description:
What happens when the darkest night of the year gets the brightest celebration? Diwali. The Festival of Lights is celebrated by millions worldwide, bringing together diyas, lanterns, rangoli, prayers, sweets, and family gatherings.
The name Diwali comes from the Sanskrit 'dipavali,' meaning 'row of lights.' The celebration falls on Amavasya, the new-moon night in the Hindu month of Kartik. Across India, the festival carries different stories and traditions. In North India, it marks Lord Rama's return to Ayodhya; in parts of South India and Nepal, it is linked to Lord Krishna's victory over Narakasura. In Bengal, the festival honors the goddess Kali. Jains and Sikhs also observe Diwali for important religious reasons.
The festival has found a home in America, too. California, Connecticut, and Pennsylvania recognize Diwali as a state holiday. The White House has hosted Diwali celebrations, while the US Postal Service has issued commemorative Diwali stamps, including one in 2026. From community events to sweets shared at schools and workplaces, Diwali continues to light up communities.

title: Historic district of Triana, Seville, Spain
caption: Where art finds its rhythm
subtitle: Historic district of Triana, Seville, Spain
description:
Cross the Guadalquivir River in Seville, the capital of Spain's Andalusia region, and the city's rhythm seems to change. On the other side lies Triana, a colorful neighborhood where ceramics, flamenco, and local traditions are woven into everyday life. Since the 19th century, the Isabel II Bridge, also known as the Triana Bridge, has connected the neighborhood to Seville's historic center.
Step off the bridge and Triana's distinctive character comes into view. The neighborhood has a long tradition of pottery and tilemaking, and colorful azulejos still brighten facades and workshops. Its streets have also played an important role in the history of flamenco, an art form deeply associated with Triana. Along Calle Betis, brightly painted buildings face the Guadalquivir.
Triana isn't defined by a single monument. Its appeal lies in its mix of artisans and markets, music and tiled courtyards, riverside terraces, and narrow streets. Seville may be just across the water, but Triana has a spirit all its own.

title: Aerial view of Rose Island, The Bahamas
caption: Licensed to chill
subtitle: Aerial view of Rose Island, The Bahamas
description:
From above, Rose Island looks like a brushstroke of green surrounded by every shade of blue. Just three miles east of Paradise Island in The Bahamas, this slender cay trades busy roads and city blocks for sandy shores, shallow waters, and an inland lagoon. Its peaceful appearance comes with a touch of movie drama. Rose Island was used as a filming location for the 1965 James Bond adventure 'Thunderball,' including the explosive destruction of the Disco Volante.
Beyond its cinematic cameo, Rose Island offers a glimpse of what makes The Bahamas so striking. The island is known for its swimming pigs, adding an unexpected touch of character to its shores. Across the archipelago, low-lying islands and cays meet reefs, sandbars, and brilliant shallows. Pale sand beneath clear water creates ribbons of turquoise, aquamarine, and deep blue. From this height, land and sea seem to blur together, proving that sometimes the best view of paradise comes from above.

title: American flags in a public park in upstate New York
caption: A salute in red, white, and blue
subtitle: Veterans Day
description:
As the sun filters through autumn trees in an upstate New York park, rows of flags turn the landscape into a tribute. Veterans Day, observed every November 11, honors all who have served in the US Armed Forces.
The date carries history. The armistice that ended fighting on the Western Front in World War I took effect at the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month in 1918. More than a century later, communities mark November 11 with ceremonies, parades, flag displays, and other tributes to veterans. At Arlington National Cemetery, the National Veterans Day Ceremony begins at 11 AM with a wreath-laying at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.
Tributes also happen closer to home, in schools, neighborhoods, and public spaces like the park pictured here. Whether through a community gathering, a flag raised in recognition, or a word of thanks, Veterans Day offers a moment to pause, reflect, and recognize generations of service.

title: North Window, Arches National Park, Moab, Utah
caption: Architecture without an architect
subtitle: North Window, Arches National Park, Moab, Utah
description:
On November 12, Arches National Park marks the anniversary of its designation as a national park in 1971. Just north of Moab, Utah, the high-desert park is home to more than 2,000 natural sandstone arches—the densest concentration of arches in the world. Today's image, North Window, is one of the best-known formations in the park's Windows Section, where towering fins, openings, and sculpted sandstone create a landscape that looks almost architectural.
North Window certainly has the look of a giant stone gateway, framing distant cliffs and ever-changing skies. But there was no blueprint, architect, or construction crew involved. Instead, water, ice, temperature changes, and gravity gradually wore away softer rock, leaving the tougher layers behind.
More than five decades after becoming a national park, Arches still proves that nature can be one spectacular architect—with a very, very long construction schedule.

title: Abraham Lake in Alberta, Canada
caption: Hidden depths
subtitle: Ice on Abraham Lake in Alberta, Canada
description: Dawn's first light is reflected on the frozen surface of Abraham Lake, framed by peaks of the Rocky Mountains. In winter, this picturesque lake in Alberta is famous for its frozen bubbles of methane gas, trapped beneath the ice. Strong winds keep the surface clear of snow, offering winter-long views. Come spring, when the ice thaws, the gas escapes into the atmosphere. Despite its natural beauty, the lake is a human-made reservoir, created in 1972 when the Bighorn Dam was built on the North Saskatchewan River. Its icy beauty in winter and turquoise waters in summer make it a popular photography spot all year round.

title: Victoria Harbour, Hong Kong, China
caption: The only way is up
description: Welcome to Hong Kong, home to the world's largest collection of skyscrapers. Those pictured here tower above Victoria Harbour, whose deep waters allowed the island to develop as a busy trading port. Ships carrying tea, silk, and other goods have passed through since the 1840s, but growth rocketed in the decades after World War II, fueling a construction boom. With little flat land available between the harbor and the hills, developers had to build upward, creating this distinctive skyline. In 2026, Hong Kong has 569 buildings above 492 feet high—more than any other city.
